# `ref`, `ptr`, and `nil`

The objects chapter stopped right before the question that comes up most often: where is the data
actually stored? `Person(name: "Ada")` on a `ref object` puts the data on the heap and keeps a
pointer to it. On a plain `object`, the data sits directly inside the variable. This chapter opens
that box: `ref`, `ptr`, and `nil`.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can allocate a `ref` with `new`, read fields through automatic
dereferencing, use `ptr` with `addr`, test for `nil` with `isNil`, and explain when `ptr` is needed
and what it risks.
:::

## `ref`: data lives on the heap

A `ref object` stores its data on the heap. The variable only holds a pointer to it.

```{.nim}
type Person = ref object
  name: string
  age: int

var p: Person
new(p)
p.name = "Ada"
p.age = 36
echo p.name, " is ", p.age
```

```{.txt}
Ada is 36
```

`var p: Person` does not point at any object yet; its value is `nil`. `new(p)` asks the heap for
memory, builds an object with every field at its default, then stores the address in `p`. After
that the fields can be assigned like any object.

The constructor literal shortens those two steps. `Person(name: "Ada", age: 36)` allocates and
fills the fields at once.

## Automatic dereferencing

The value a `ref` points at is reached with `p[]`.

```{.nim}
type Person = ref object
  name: string

var p = Person(name: "Ada")

echo p.name
echo p[].name
```

```{.txt}
Ada
Ada
```

Both lines do the same thing. The compiler inserts a dereference when you write `p.name` on a
`ref`. `p[]` is the explicit form, and the rule is general: `p.age`, `p.name`, and so on, without
writing `[]` every time.

## `nil` and `isNil`

`nil` means "pointing at no object". A `ref` declared without an initial value holds `nil`.

```{.nim}
type Node = ref object
  value: int

var a: Node
echo a.isNil

a = Node(value: 7)
echo a.isNil
echo a.value
```

```{.txt}
true
false
7
```

`isNil` returns `true` while the reference is empty. Once it is filled in, the result is `false`.
Test `isNil` before using a reference that may not be set yet. Dereferencing `nil` stops the
program while it runs, not while it compiles: on macOS and Linux the process dies with `SIGSEGV`,
not with a Nim exception you can catch in `try`.

## `ptr`: an address, not an owner

`ptr T` holds the address of a location of type `T`. The `addr` operator takes the address, and
`p[]` reads it.

```{.nim}
var x = 42
var p: ptr int = addr x

echo p[]
p[] = 100
echo x
```

```{.txt}
42
100
```

`p` points at `x`. Reading `p[]` gives the value of `x`, and writing `p[] = 100` changes `x`. Both
share the same location, so a change through `p` is visible in `x` at once.

A `ptr` owns no memory. It only records an address. Nim does not free the memory a `ptr` points
at, because ownership lives somewhere else.

`ptr` works on objects too:

```{.nim}
type Counter = object
  hits: int

var c = Counter(hits: 0)
var pc = addr c

pc[].hits = 3
echo c.hits
```

```{.txt}
3
```

`addr c` takes the address of `c`; `pc[].hits = 3` changes the field through the pointer, and
`c.hits` changes with it.

## `addr` and `unsafeAddr`

`addr` only works on addressable locations. A `var` plainly has one; for `let` and parameters, Nim
still allows it for better interop with C.

```{.nim}
let year = 2008
let p = addr year

echo p[]
```

```{.txt}
2008
```

`unsafeAddr` is an old alias for `addr`, and the `system.nim` docs in 2.2.12 already mark it
deprecated. The compiler does not always emit a warning when you use it, so prefer `addr` in new
code.

## `cast` in brief

`cast` reinterprets the bits of a value as another type, without changing the bits.

```{.nim}
echo cast[uint8]('A')
```

```{.txt}
65
```

`'A'` is stored as the byte `65`, and `cast[uint8]` reads it as a number. `cast` does not change
the value; it reinterprets the same bits. Compare `cast[int32](3.5'f32)`, which yields
`1080033280`, the float's bits read as an `int32`. To convert with the language's rules, use
`int(x)`, `float(x)`, or `$x`; save `cast` for low-level code.

## Reading an error: expression has no address

`addr` demands a fixed location. A literal has none, so its address cannot be taken.

```{.nim}
var p = addr 42
echo p[]
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(1, 14) Error: expression has no address
```

Position `(1, 14)` points at the literal `42` in `addr 42`, not at the `addr` token itself; the
message then states the problem: that expression has no address. The fix is to store the value in a
variable first, then take the address of that variable.

## `ref object` vs `object`

The difference shows up most clearly when a value is copied.

| Aspect | `object` | `ref object` |
|---|---|---|
| data is stored in | the variable itself | the heap |
| what the variable holds | the data directly | a pointer |
| copying means | duplicating the data | duplicating the pointer |
| default value | each field's default | `nil` |

`ref object` is used when several parts of the code must share one value, or when the data is
large. `object` is used for small values that are meant to be copied. The copying details were
covered in the objects chapter.

## When `ptr` is needed, and its risks

`ptr` is needed to talk to C, to write low-level procedures, or to point into a buffer. Beyond
that, `ref` is almost always better because its memory is managed automatically.

The risks are real:

- **Dangling.** The address of a local variable becomes invalid the moment its block ends. The
  `ptr` does not know that.
- **Unchecked.** A `ptr` can point anywhere; Nim does not check bounds or types while the program
  runs.
- **`nil` left untested.** Dereferencing a `ptr` or `ref` that is `nil` stops the program with
  `SIGSEGV`, not with an exception.

So the rule is simple: use `ref` when you can, and reach for `ptr` only when there is no choice.

## Exercises

1. Allocate a `ref object` `Book` with a `title` field, create two instances with `new`, then print
   both titles.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   type Point = ref object
     x, y: int

   var p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
   var q = p
   q.x = 10
   echo p.x, " ", q.x
   ```
3. Write a procedure `incr(p: ptr int)` that increases the value pointed at by `p` by one.
4. Why must `var p: Person` go through `new(p)` before `p.name` can be assigned?
5. The code below fails to compile. Fix it, then explain the error message:
   ```{.nim}
   var x = 5
   var p: ptr int = x
   echo p[]
   ```

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- A `ref object` stores data on the heap; `p.name` already dereferences for you.
- `new(p)` allocates a `ref` that was still `nil`; `isNil` tests whether the reference is empty.
- `ptr T` holds an address, taken with `addr` and read with `p[]`; `unsafeAddr` is its deprecated
  alias.
- `cast` reinterprets bits, it does not convert the value; use it only in low-level code.
- A `ptr` owns no memory and is unchecked, so prefer `ref` whenever you can.
